cards.definition: The provision of food, drink, accommodation and entertainment to guests, customers or visitors.
The business of providing food and drink at events, in institutions, or at commercial establishments.
Hospitality and catering businesses that operate to make a profit, e.g. restaurants, hotels and fast-food chains.
Hospitality and catering provision not primarily run for profit, e.g. hospitals, schools and care homes.
The area of a hospitality business where customers are served, including reception, dining room and bar.
The area of a hospitality business not visible to customers, including kitchens, stores and offices.
A set menu offering a limited number of courses at a fixed price, commonly used in restaurants and hotels.
A menu where each dish is individually priced and customers choose from a wide selection.
Positions within the industry range from executive chef and hotel manager to waiting staff and kitchen porter.
The assistance and experience provided to customers before, during and after their visit to ensure satisfaction.
French for 'putting in place'; the preparation of ingredients, equipment and the kitchen before service begins.
Revenue minus the cost of food and drink sold; a key measure of a catering business's profitability.
Measuring or standardising the amount of food served per customer to control costs and ensure consistency.
Food or ingredients that are discarded or spoiled, increasing costs and reducing profitability.
A menu that changes according to the time of year, featuring ingredients that are in season and therefore fresher and cheaper.
Current developments in the industry such as plant-based menus, sustainable sourcing, technology ordering and health-conscious dining.
A business model where an operator runs a branch under an established brand's name and systems, e.g. McDonald's.
A business owned and run by one person who takes all the profits and bears all the risks.
The number of employees needed to operate a hospitality business efficiently at different times of day or year.
The hours during which a hospitality business is open to customers; affects staffing, supplies and profitability.
Illness caused by eating contaminated food, typically producing symptoms such as nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea.
Microscopic organisms that can multiply rapidly in food and cause food poisoning; examples include Salmonella and E. coli.
The temperature range between 5°C and 63°C in which bacteria multiply most rapidly in food.
The transfer of harmful bacteria from one food or surface to another, often via hands, equipment or raw meat.
Practices that prevent contamination of food, including handwashing, wearing clean protective clothing and covering cuts.
Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points; a food safety management system that identifies and controls hazards in food production.
A step in food preparation where a hazard can be controlled or eliminated, e.g. cooking to a safe core temperature.
Foods that support the rapid growth of bacteria, such as cooked meat, dairy products, seafood and cooked rice.
Common causes include Salmonella (poultry), Campylobacter (chicken), Listeria (soft cheese) and Staphylococcus aureus (skin contact).
The internal temperature food must reach to destroy harmful bacteria; typically 75°C for at least 2 minutes.
UK law (based on EU Regulation 852/2004) requiring food businesses to ensure food is produced, handled and stored safely.
A local authority inspector who checks that food businesses comply with food safety and hygiene legislation.
The government body responsible for food safety and hygiene standards in the UK.
A public rating (0–5 stars) given to food businesses after EHO inspection, displayed to inform consumers.
First In, First Out — using older stock before newer deliveries to reduce wastage and ensure freshness.
The date after which a food product should not be eaten due to food safety risks; a legal requirement on high-risk foods.
The date up to which a food product is at its best quality; after this date it may be safe but of lower quality.
Measures to prevent or eliminate pests such as rats, mice and insects from food premises to avoid contamination.
A calibrated thermometer inserted into food to check its core temperature has reached a safe level.
A written plan specifying what surfaces or equipment must be cleaned, how, and how often, to maintain hygienic premises.
Nutrients needed in large amounts for energy and body function: carbohydrates, proteins and fats.
Vitamins and minerals needed in small amounts for health; they do not provide energy but support body functions.
A macronutrient needed for growth, repair and maintenance of body tissues; found in meat, fish, eggs, pulses and dairy.
The body's main energy source; divided into simple sugars (quick energy) and complex starches (slow-release energy).
A macronutrient providing energy, insulation and fat-soluble vitamins; saturated fats are linked to heart disease.
Non-starch polysaccharide; aids digestion and helps prevent constipation and bowel disease.
A water-soluble vitamin essential for the immune system and iron absorption; found in citrus fruits and vegetables.
A fat-soluble vitamin needed for calcium absorption and bone health; obtained from sunlight, oily fish and eggs.
A mineral needed for haemoglobin in red blood cells; deficiency causes anaemia. Found in red meat, spinach and lentils.
A mineral essential for strong bones and teeth and for nerve and muscle function; found in dairy, fortified plant milks and leafy greens.
A UK government guide showing the proportions of different food groups needed for a balanced diet.
The amount of a nutrient that is sufficient to meet the needs of most of the population.
A medical condition caused by excessive body fat, linked to overconsumption of energy-dense foods and insufficient activity.
A condition where the body cannot regulate blood sugar effectively, often linked to poor diet and obesity.
Diseases of the heart and blood vessels, often linked to high saturated fat and salt intake.
A diet that excludes meat and fish; must be carefully planned to ensure adequate protein, iron and B12.
A diet excluding all animal products; requires careful planning for protein, iron, calcium, vitamin B12 and vitamin D.
An adverse reaction to a specific food that does not involve the immune system, e.g. lactose intolerance.
An immune system reaction to a food protein; the 14 major allergens include nuts, gluten, dairy and shellfish.
Information on food packaging showing energy, fat, saturated fat, carbohydrate, sugar, protein and salt content per 100g.
The specific group of customers a business aims to serve, e.g. families, business clients or health-conscious diners.
The nutritional needs or food restrictions of a customer, such as allergies, intolerances, or religious and ethical preferences.
Calculating the cost of all ingredients used in a recipe to determine the selling price and profit margin.
The price a customer pays for a dish; must cover ingredient costs, overheads, staff and profit.
The ratio of ingredient cost to selling price, expressed as a percentage; typically 25–35% in the catering industry.
Ensuring that a menu offers dishes that together provide a range of macro and micronutrients for a healthy diet.
Using a variety of colours and plating techniques to make dishes visually appealing and professional-looking.
Flavours that work well together, e.g. lemon with fish, or mint with lamb, to create a balanced dish.
Combining different textures in a dish (e.g. crunchy croutons on smooth soup) to add variety and interest.
Offering dishes prepared by different methods (roasting, steaming, grilling) to give customers range and avoid repetition.
Menus that cater for specific needs such as gluten-free, halal, kosher, vegan or low-calorie requirements.
Businesses must clearly declare the 14 major allergens in dishes, either on the menu or via staff; required by law.
The origin of food ingredients; customers increasingly expect information about where food has been sourced.
Obtaining ingredients from local suppliers to reduce food miles, support local farmers and improve freshness.
Analysing the profitability and popularity of each dish to decide which items to promote, keep or remove.
A menu item that is both popular with customers and highly profitable; a key focus of menu engineering.
The number of customers served in a service period; covers per hour is a measure of restaurant efficiency.
The time between one group of customers leaving a table and the next group being seated; affects revenue.
Encouraging customers to purchase higher-value items or extras, e.g. a dessert or premium wine.
The usable portion of an ingredient after trimming, peeling or cooking; important for accurate costing.
A container of hot water used to keep food warm or to melt ingredients gently without direct heat.
A kitchen tool with an adjustable blade used to slice vegetables thinly and evenly.
Equipment that rapidly reduces the temperature of cooked food to below 5°C, preventing bacterial growth.
A commercial oven that combines conventional heat, steam and fan-forced heat for versatile cooking methods.
A commercial overhead grill used for browning, glazing and finishing dishes quickly.
Different coloured boards used for different food types to prevent cross-contamination, e.g. red for raw meat, green for salad.
Procedures to prevent injury when using kitchen knives, including keeping knives sharp, using a guard and storing safely.
Clothing and equipment to protect workers in the kitchen, such as oven gloves, aprons and non-slip footwear.
Control of Substances Hazardous to Health — regulations covering safe storage, use and disposal of chemicals in the kitchen.
A formal process of identifying potential hazards in the kitchen and putting measures in place to reduce or eliminate them.
Cooking without water or moisture, e.g. roasting, baking, grilling and frying.
Cooking using water or steam, e.g. boiling, steaming, poaching and braising.
Cooking food uncovered in an oven using fat; suitable for large joints of meat and root vegetables.
Cooking food under or over direct radiant heat; quick and suitable for meat, fish and vegetables.
Cooking food using steam from boiling water; preserves nutrients and colour better than boiling.
Slow-cooking food in a small amount of liquid in a covered pan; ideal for tougher cuts of meat.
Cooking food by fully submerging it in hot oil; produces a crispy exterior. Requires temperature control for safety.
Cooking food in a small amount of fat in a pan; suitable for fish, eggs and thin cuts of meat.
Gently cooking food in simmering liquid (below boiling point); suitable for eggs, fish and fruit.
Cooking vacuum-sealed food in a precisely controlled water bath; produces consistent results and retains moisture.
The distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is eaten; shorter food miles reduce carbon emissions.
Producing and consuming food in a way that meets current needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
Food grown without synthetic pesticides or fertilisers and with high animal welfare standards; certified by bodies like the Soil Association.
A certification ensuring producers in developing countries receive a fair price and decent working conditions for their goods.
Food that is grown and harvested at a particular time of year; seasonal produce is fresher, cheaper and has lower food miles.
The complete journey of food from production on the farm through processing, distribution and retail to the consumer.
A UK food assurance scheme that guarantees food has been produced to UK standards of food safety, animal welfare and environmental protection.
Strategies to minimise food thrown away, including stock rotation, portion control, creative use of trimmings and composting.
The total greenhouse gas emissions caused by the production, transport and consumption of food.
A diet centred on plant foods with little or no animal products; generally has a lower environmental impact than meat-heavy diets.
